title: Teachers Received a Random Genius List, Yet Young Kids Jumped Fifteen IQ Points
description:
Myth vs. Neural Mechanism — Robert Rosenthal & Lenore Jacobson (1966-1968): Oak School 'Pygmalion in the Classroom' Self-Fulfilling Prophecy, grounded in Robert Rosenthal, Lenore Jacobson (1966) (Psychological Reports). Empirical findings show that in spring 1964 (published 1966 in Psychological Reports and 1968 as Pygmalion in the Classroom), Robert Rosenthal and principal Lenore Jacobson tested all pupils across 18 classrooms (grades 1-6) at 'Oak School' in South San Francisco.

Follow-up physiological and behavioral evidence demonstrates: Students took a standard nonverbal IQ test (Flanagan's Tests of General Ability), but teachers were told it was a brand-new 'Harvard Test of Inflected Acquisition' predicting imminent intellectual 'spurting'.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Robert Rosenthal, Lenore Jacobson (1966). Teachers' Expectancies: Determinants of Pupils' IQ Gains. Psychological Reports. https://doi.org/10.2466/pr0.1966.19.1.115

- Jacques Lecomte (2019). Robert Rosenthal. L'effet Pygmalion. Les Grands Dossiers des Sciences Humaines. https://doi.org/10.3917/gdsh.0054.0018
